title: The Patents Act, 1970 - Section 3(p)
authority: Parliament of India / Office of Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
text: Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970 specifies that an invention which in effect, is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known component or components is NOT an invention within the meaning of this Act and cannot be granted a patent in India. In Ayurveda, this explicitly bars patenting known classical formulations or established traditional uses of medicinal herbs (such as Ashwagandha, Turmeric, Neem) unless substantial, unexpected synergistic efficacy and inventive novelty are proven beyond mere traditional aggregation.

title: The Patents Act, 1970 - Section 3(e)
text: Section 3(e) states that a substance obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the properties of the components thereof or a process for producing such substance is NOT patentable. For herbal and Ayurvedic formulations, merely mixing known herbs (e.g. Ashwagandha + Brahmi) without demonstrable synergistic effect or a unique, unobvious technical interaction will be rejected under Section 3(e) as an unpatentable mere admixture.

title: The Patents Act, 1970 - Section 3(d)
text: Section 3(d) excludes the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in the enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance, or the mere discovery of any new property or new use for a known substance. When isolating botanical active compounds or standardizing extracts from known Ayurvedic plants, the applicant must demonstrate significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy over the known herbal extract to overcome Section 3(d).

title: The Patents Act, 1970 - Section 10(4)(d)(ii) & Biological Material Disclosure
text: Section 10(4)(d)(ii) mandates that if the patent specification mentions biological material used in an invention, the applicant must disclose the source and geographical origin of the biological material in India. Non-disclosure or wrongful disclosure of geographical origin is a statutory ground for pre-grant opposition under Section 25(1)(j), post-grant opposition under Section 25(2)(j), and revocation under Section 64(1)(p).

title: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 - Section 6 (Prior Approval for IPR)
authority: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
chapter: Chapter II - Regulation of Access to Biological Diversity
text: Section 6(1) provides that no person shall apply for any intellectual property right, by whatever name called, in or outside India for any invention based on any research or information on a biological resource obtained from India without obtaining the previous approval of the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) prior to grant of patent. Under the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023, approval must be obtained before the grant of the patent, but prior application is permitted. Form III must be filed with NBA.

title: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 - Section 3 & Section 7 (Access and SBB Intimation)
chapter: Chapter II - Regulation of Access to Biological Diversity
text: Section 3 requires non-Indian citizens, non-residents, or foreign-controlled entities to obtain prior approval from the NBA (Form I) before accessing any biological resource occurring in India or associated knowledge for research, commercial utilization, or bio-survey. Section 7 requires Indian citizens and entities to give prior intimation to the concerned State Biodiversity Board (SBB) before obtaining biological resources for commercial utilization, except local people, vaids, and hakims practicing indigenous medicine.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 - Section 3(a) (Classical Ayurvedic Drugs)
authority: Ministry of Ayush / Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO)
text: Section 3(a) defines 'Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug' as including all medicines intended for internal or external use for diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder in human beings or animals, and manufactured exclusively in accordance with the formulae described in the authoritative books of Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani systems of medicine specified in the First Schedule. These are classical generic formulations (e.g. Triphala Churna, Chyawanprash as per Charaka Samhita).

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 - Section 3(h) (Patent or Proprietary Medicine)
text: Section 3(h)(i) defines 'Patent or Proprietary Medicine' in relation to Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani systems as a drug which is a formulation containing only ingredients mentioned in the formulae described in the authoritative books of Ayurveda, Siddha or Unani specified in the First Schedule, but which is NOT a formulation described in the First Schedule texts itself. Such proprietary medicines require licensing under Rule 158B with proof of safety, trial data or established textual rationale.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 - Rule 158B (Licensing Guidelines for ASU Drugs)
authority: Ministry of Ayush, Government of India
chapter: Part XVI - Manufacture for Sale of ASU Drugs
text: Rule 158B prescribes requirements for issue of license for manufacturing Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drugs. For classical drugs (Section 3(a)), only textual references are needed. For Patent or Proprietary drugs (Section 3(h)), it categorizes products into: Category A (classical text ingredients with new indications, requiring pilot clinical study or textual justification), Category B (ingredients from authoritative books combined for existing indications, requiring safety evidence), and Category C (extracts/novel aqueous extracts requiring acute toxicity and safety reports).

title: Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahar) Regulations, 2022
authority: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) & Ministry of Ayush
text: Ayurveda Aahar covers food prepared in accordance with recipes or ingredients described in authoritative books of Ayurveda listed in Schedule A of these regulations, intended to promote health and well-being. It does NOT include Ayurvedic drugs covered under Chapter IV-A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, nor does it include synthetic vitamins, minerals, or amino acids. Labels must carry the special Ayurveda Aahar logo and mandatory disclaimer: 'NOT FOR MEDICINAL USE - PROMOTES GENERAL HEALTH'.

title: Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 - Rule 122E (Phytopharmaceutical Drugs)
text: A Phytopharmaceutical Drug is defined as purified and standardized fraction with defined minimum four bioactive/analytical marker compounds of an extract of a medicinal plant or its part, for internal or external use of human beings or animals for diagnosis, treatment, mitigation, or prevention of any disease or disorder. Unlike classical Ayurveda medicines, phytopharmaceuticals follow the allopathic new drug regulatory route, requiring Phase I/II/III clinical trials, IND approval, and full CMC dossiers under CDSCO oversight.

title: WTO TRIPS Agreement - Article 27 (Patentable Subject Matter)
text: Article 27.1 provides that patents shall be available for any inventions, whether products or processes, in all fields of technology, provided that they are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application. Article 27.2 permits members to exclude inventions where prevention of commercial exploitation is necessary to protect ordre public or morality, including human, animal or plant life. Article 27.3(b) permits members to exclude plants and animals other than micro-organisms, and essentially biological processes for the production of plants or animals.

title: Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and Benefit-Sharing
authority: Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
text: The Nagoya Protocol implements the third objective of the CBD: fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources and traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources. Users of genetic resources or traditional knowledge must obtain Prior Informed Consent (PIC) from the provider country/indigenous community and establish Mutually Agreed Terms (MAT) specifying benefit-sharing mechanisms before commercial exploitation or patenting in member states.

title: WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge
text: Adopted in Geneva on May 24, 2024, this landmark WIPO Treaty establishes a mandatory disclosure requirement in patent applications. Where an invention claimed in a patent application is based on genetic resources, applicants must disclose the country of origin or source. Where based on traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources, applicants must disclose the Indigenous Peoples or local community that provided the traditional knowledge. This internationalizes prior-art checks and prevents biopiracy of traditional medicinal knowledge like Ayurveda.

title: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) & Prior Art Directives
authority: Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) & Ministry of Ayush
text: TKDL bridges classical Sanskrit/Arabic/Persian texts into structured patent classifications (IPC) in five international languages (English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish). Access agreements exist with major patent offices (USPTO, EPO, JPO, UKIPO, IP Australia, CGPDTM) allowing patent examiners to verify that an Ayurvedic formula is already recorded in the public domain prior art, triggering rapid rejection of misappropriated patent claims under Section 3(p) or novelty rules.

title: Trade Marks Act, 1999 - Section 9 (Absolute Grounds for Refusal)
chapter: Chapter II - Grounds for Refusal of Registration
text: Section 9(1)(b) states that trademarks which consist exclusively of signs or indications which may serve in trade to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, values, or geographical origin of goods cannot be registered. Generic Ayurvedic terms, classical plant names (e.g., 'Ashwagandha', 'Triphala', 'Brahmi'), or traditional preparation names cannot be registered as private trademarks because they are descriptive and common to the trade.
